preamble: Fronting of the voiced postalveolar affricate [dʒ] to the alveolar affricate [dz]. Marathi has [dz] for the inherited Middle Indo-Aryan j (Maharashtri Prakrit ajja 'today' > आज /ad͡z/). In Polish dialects with mazurzenie (Masovia, Masuria, most of Lesser Poland, parts of Silesia), the older soft palato-alveolar /d͡ʒ/ (dż) merged with /d͡z/ when the series lost its palatalization around the 16th century, while the standard language and the other dialects turned it into retroflex /d͡ʐ/. So drożdże 'yeast' is drozdze in Zagórze, and the standard language has the mazurated dzban 'jug' for Old Polish dżban or czban. Wikipedia (Mazuration, after Dejna, Kuraszkiewicz and Rospond) says that in these dialects "the postalveolar sibilants merged completely with the dentialveolars", and Koneczna derives the merger directly from the depalatalization. In Kuryłowicz's account the archaic dialects, trying to adopt the neighbours' new retroflex /ʂ ʐ/, replaced them with the /s z/ they already had. For the affricates, English Wikipedia reports Kuryłowicz as saying that /t͡ʂ d͡ʐ/ then coalesced with /t͡s d͡z/, while Polish Wikipedia gives /t͡ʃ d͡ʒ/, both citing Milewski (1956: 49–50); since the other accounts derive the dentals directly from the palato-alveolars, the change is filed here as direct. Stieber (cited by Wikipedia) considers the phonemic status of [d͡ʒʲ] in Old Polish doubtful. Old Polish had soft palato-alveolars (/t͡ʃʲ ʃʲ ʒʲ d͡ʒʲ/ in Wiktionary's transcription); they are filed here under the plain symbols.

languageExamples.language: Old Polish to Polish (mazurzenie dialects and a mazurated standard form)

examples.note: Zagórze drozdze is the dialect form of Polish drożdże 'yeast', which Wiktionary derives from Old Polish drożdża; both dż and ż are fronted.

Wikipedia (Mazuration, after Kuraszkiewicz 1972) gives dzban "instead of Old Polish dżban/czban"; Wiktionary derives dzban from Proto-Slavic *čьbanъ, lists Old Polish czban and zban, and calls the current form "a result of mazuration".
